summary:
Tomsk Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, where the legal and physical risks for transgender visitors are severe. In 2023 the Russian government prohibited gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents, effectively banning trans-specific healthcare; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded "propaganda" law criminalises public expression including anything that "justifies" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and official Russian government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this. The US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) sets out the national framework as it applies to Tomsk Oblast: same-sex marriage and legal gender transition are banned, trans-specific healthcare has been effectively banned since 2023, and no discrimination protection is available to transgender people. The same note records 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws across Russia between 2022 and 2024. It records no facts specific to Tomsk Oblast.

That note assesses that lesbian, gay and bisexual people are not generally at real risk of persecution solely on the basis of sexual orientation, while people in the North Caucasus, transgender people and public LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. For a trans visitor the practical consequence is exposure to the extremist-designation regime and to the propaganda statutes, under which display, advocacy or discussion can be charged as participation in a banned organisation.

Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the "International LGBT Movement" or for displaying its symbols, comprising 98 administrative and 3 criminal convictions, with at least 20 people facing criminal charges from January 2024 onward. Three staff of a publishing house charged on 15 May 2025 face up to 12 years' imprisonment, and repeated display of the banned symbols carries up to four years.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement volume has risen alongside severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget over two years. The Guardian documented on 17 January 2024 that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, with about 100 patrons at one venue ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues raided the same night.

Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to people fleeing Russia. The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, including a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as a second-class citizen after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Coercive practices targeting transgender people are documented at the parent-nation level: BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that a transgender woman was lured in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk in Siberia, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping. Incidents of this kind illustrate a pattern that a visitor to Tomsk Oblast would be subject to under the same national statutes, though none of these cases occurred in the oblast.
localsOnly:
Residents of Tomsk Oblast have no legal route to change gender markers on official documents, and no access to gender-affirming medical care through lawful channels since the 2023 prohibition. Same-sex marriage is not recognised, and no anti-discrimination protection covers transgender people in employment, housing, healthcare or public services.

Human Rights Watch's count of 101 extremism-related convictions by June 2025, 98 administrative and 3 criminal, applies to residents as well as visitors, as does the risk of charges for displaying or sharing symbols associated with the designated organisation. Repeated display of those symbols carries up to four years' imprisonment; the three publishing-house staff charged on 15 May 2025 face up to 12 years.

The UK Home Office note treats LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, as a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. Residents considering departure on those grounds would be assessed against that standard.
outOfScopeNotes:
No facts specific to Tomsk Oblast appear in the sources used here, including the UK Home Office note; all legal and enforcement findings derive from the Russian national framework and are cited as such. Whether oblast-level police units have conducted raids, issued propaganda-law fines or brought extremism charges is not sourced and remains unresolved.

Local statistics on hate crimes, detention or violence against transgender residents of Tomsk Oblast are not sourced. The availability of legal aid, support organisations or safe accommodation within the oblast is likewise not addressed by the inventory. The status of any oblast-level protective measures, if any exist, is unresolved for the same reason.
